text:
**Let the Parking Mandates Go**

Walk through almost any American city and you will find a quiet rule shaping what gets built. It is the minimum parking requirement. It says a restaurant must provide so many spaces per thousand square feet, an apartment building so many per unit, a dentist's office so many per examination room. Developers do not get to decide how much parking their customers need. The city decides for them. Cities should repeal these rules, and the sooner the better.

Start with the premise behind the mandate: that without it, nobody would build enough parking. This is odd on its face. Businesses already want customers, and customers who drive need somewhere to leave the car. A grocery store with no parking in a car-dependent suburb would fail, and its owner knows it. Remove the requirement and that store will still build a lot. What changes is the cases where the requirement is plainly wrong: the corner cafe in a walkable neighborhood, the apartment block beside a train station, the small business moving into an old building that has no room for a lot.

Those cases matter because the rules are blunt. The numbers in most codes come from manuals built on thin samples, often surveys of suburban sites with ample free parking. Planners then treat the peak demand observed at those sites as a floor for everyone. The result is lots sized for the busiest hour of the busiest day, which sit mostly empty the rest of the year. Anyone who has seen a vast, vacant lot on a Tuesday afternoon has seen the outcome.

Empty asphalt is not free. Structured parking can cost tens of thousands of dollars per space to build, and underground garages cost more. Surface lots eat land that could hold homes or shops. Those costs do not vanish; they land in rents, in menu prices, and in the units that never get built because the numbers stopped working. A requirement of one or two spaces per apartment can consume a large share of a small lot, killing modest projects before they start. Housing is scarce and expensive in much of the country. Making every new home arrive bundled with a car's storage is a strange way to respond.

There is also the matter of fairness. When parking is required and bundled into the rent, a household without a car still pays for the space. Lower-income renters, who are more likely to go without a car, subsidize the parking of their wealthier neighbors. Free parking is not free. Someone pays for it, and they are rarely the people using it most.

Consider what the rules do to the shape of a city. Mandates spread buildings apart to make room for lots. Greater distances make walking unpleasant and transit unworkable, which makes driving more necessary, which seems to justify more parking. The loop feeds itself. Historic downtowns, with their tight blocks and shared street parking, would be illegal to build under many modern codes. We prize those places and then prohibit making more of them.

Critics raise real objections, and they deserve answers. The first is spillover: if developers build less parking, cars will clog the neighborhood streets. Sometimes that happens. But the remedy for crowded curbs is to manage the curb, not to force every building to hoard private spaces. Residential permit programs and priced on-street parking handle this well. A city that charges a fair price for scarce curb space gets turnover, availability, and revenue it can spend on the neighborhood.

The second objection is that some people really do need to drive: the elderly, people with disabilities, workers in shift jobs with no transit at that hour. True, and nothing in repeal takes their needs away. Accessible spaces can stay mandatory under separate rules, and developers serving those residents will still build parking. Repeal does not ban parking. It returns the decision to the people who bear the cost and know the market.

The evidence from cities that have tried it is encouraging. Buffalo eliminated its citywide minimums in 2017, and others, including Minneapolis, Anchorage, and a growing list of smaller places, have followed. These cities did not become car-free wastelands or gridlocked messes. Developers still build parking where it pays. What they gained is flexibility: small infill projects, adaptive reuse of old buildings, and more homes on the same land.

Some caution is fair. Repeal alone will not fix housing costs, and it will not make a sprawling suburb walkable overnight. Other rules, from height caps to setbacks, also need attention. But removing minimums is among the cheapest reforms available. It costs the city nothing, requires no new subsidy, and relies on a simple idea: those who build and use a place know better than a rule table how much parking it needs.

A city should decide what it wants its streets, neighborhoods, and budgets to look like. A mandate that guarantees a surplus of parking is a decision made long ago by people who assumed everyone would drive everywhere forever. We can do better. Scrap the minimums, price the curb sensibly, and let the market and the neighborhood work out the rest.
